To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we provide improved approximation algorithms and approximation ratios for rectangle tiling problems.

(1) the approximation ratio of the RTILE problem can be improved from $1.5$ to $1.2$ and the approximation ratios of the DRTILE problem can be reduced from $2.2$ to $1$ and from $2$ to $2/3$ for the two versions of the problem, (2) the approximation ratio for the d-RPACK problem is $1.5$.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following problems: RTILE: Given a set of n rectangles with integer coordinates, does there exist a packing of these rectangles in a rectangle of size m x m?

the following problems: Given a finite set of rectangles, (a) find a minimum number of rectangles to cover a rectangular domain, (b) find a minimum size rectangular domain that can be covered with the given rectangles, and (c) find a maximum size rectangular sub-domain that can be covered by the given rectangles.
two fundamental problems in computational geometry and combinatorial optimization: rectangle tiling and rectangle packing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have improved approximation ratios and/or running time for all of these problems.
we provide the best known approximation algorithms for all the problems considered in this work, and that these algorithms are highly efficient.
our results are a major breakthrough for the field of geometric packing problems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we improve the approximation ratio of RTILE and DRTILE to 2.75 and 2.5 respectively, and we improve the approximation ratios of d-RPACK for d=2 and d=3 to 2.5 and 2.75 respectively.
we provide improved approximation algorithms, for several problems in RTILE, DRTile and d-RPACK, that run in near-linear time.
we provide a 1.5 approximation algorithm for RTILE and DRTILE and a 1.25 approximation algorithm for d-RPACK, for any d ≥ 1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the approximation ratios of these problems can be substantially improved by exploiting the geometric structure of the input, rather than the combinatorial structure.
, for the problems we consider, approximation algorithms that are efficient and have good approximation ratios can be obtained by a combination of the following two techniques.

, by using a combination of the classical techniques for solving RTILE, namely, dynamic programming and the greedy method, we can obtain approximation algorithms with much better performance ratios than those obtained by using only one of the two methods.
